1.pericope_label: I said, I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue: I will keep my mouth with a bridle, while the wicked is before me

schools.summary: Delitzsch pairs the psalm with the one before it, where the poet had likewise called himself a dumb man who opens not his mouth, and with a later psalm of the same historical background, all of them carrying Jeduthun's name beside David's. Ellicott supplies what the others assume — how unnatural the silence was, given the unrestrained way Orientals give way to grief — and traces the bridle to a root meaning stop, gathering James, Virgil and Plato's remark that an argument, like a horse, must be pulled up and held with bit and bridle.

Calvin takes Jeduthun for the chief singer of David's household and refuses two alternatives: that the name marks a tune, which he calls too forced, and that David complains of a particular disease, since it is improper to narrow a general statement without urgent reason. From the extremity of the suffering he infers a variety of afflictions, or one severer than the rest that had lasted long. Gill notes only that David put his resolution into practice.

Clarke reports the identification of Jeduthun with Ethan, one of the four masters of temple music, and the alternative that Jeduthun wrote the psalm himself; he fixes the occasion as the malady following the affair with Bathsheba, and gives three reasons for the silence at once — caution because of enemies, patience under affliction, watchfulness lest God be offended or adversaries given cause to speak. Wesley reduces the verse to two clauses.

Henry reads the verse as David reminding himself of covenants already made, since when we are tempted we must call to mind the vows made against that very sin; he keeps the bridle on the mouth as on a head and the muzzle as on an unruly dog. Spurgeon adds why tongue-sins matter here: if believers utter hard words of God in depression, the ungodly take them up as justification for their own courses.

Augustine takes the name in the title for the psalm's subject rather than its singer. Jeduthun translated is one over-leaping them, and those over-leaped are the people still clinging to the earth, bowed to the ground, setting their hearts on what is below and their hopes on what passes away.

debates.question: What is Jeduthun in the title?

positions.summary: The chief singer to whose company David gave the psalm — possibly Ethan, one of the four masters of temple music — though several have supposed Jeduthun wrote it himself.
Not the name of a tune, which is too forced an interpretation, but a person of David's household.
A name to be translated rather than identified: it means one over-leaping them, and names whoever has left behind those who cling to the earth.
The grievous malady that followed the transgression with Bathsheba, the psalm belonging with the one before it.
Not any single disease: it is improper to limit a general statement without urgent reason, and the extremity described suggests a variety of afflictions or one unusually long one.
A threat to the poet's dignity from those who had turned from false friends into open enemies, as in the psalms of the same background.

outliers.summary: Sets the resolution against its cultural background: it was natural and becoming for this poet to roar out his indignation, to mutter his prayers aloud, to speak on every impulse — so the decision to bear the worst mutely is a departure from what grief ordinarily looked like.

Turns the verse into a rule about renewing resolutions: having resolved to take heed to our ways we must on all occasions remind ourselves of it, for it is a covenant never to be forgotten. Fast bind, fast find.

themes: I said, I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue: I will keep my mouth with a bridle, while the wicked is before me.

2.pericope_label: I was dumb with silence, I held my peace, even from good; and my sorrow was stirred... surely every man walketh in a vain shew: surely they are disquieted in vain

schools.summary: Ellicott disputes the received rendering of verse 2 — the particle behind 'even from good' is not generally used in that sense after a verb of silence, only one passage supports it, and the context does not want it — preferring 'I held my peace without profit'. He describes repression making the flame burn fiercer until the passion breaks into words, not fretfully but as a dialogue with the ruler of destiny in which frail man wants to know the worst; and he marks verse 4 as the point from which all is that utterance. Delitzsch gives the request its logic: if life is only a few spans long, both the suffering and the prosperity of the ungodly are short.

Gill reads the request for an end as spoken in a passionate way by a man impatient of his exercises, and takes the handbreadth for a correction of the question: it was needless to ask, when life is not a yard or an ell or even a span but the breadth of four fingers.

Clarke states the case for and against complaint as a balance — it relieves the mind and calls attention off the place of suffering, yet extravagant complaint enervates the mind into a double prey — and thinks David steered clear of both extremes. His figure for the musing is vegetables heaped together, which ferment if not scattered and produce a flame consuming themselves and everything near. Wesley glosses the doubled verb, the shortness of life, and the comparison with God's everlasting duration.

Spurgeon makes the silence physical: the door of the heart shut with the fire of sorrow burning inside, silence the surest way to produce madness, the heart musing and fusing on a confusing subject until eruption was imminent. His counsel follows from it — tell your sorrow, first and most fully to God, but pouring it out before a wise and godly friend is far from wasted breath.

debates.question: What does 'I held my peace, even from good' mean?

positions.summary: The reading is suspicious: the particle is not used that way after a verb of silence, and the context does not want it. Read instead 'I held my peace without profit' — silence increased the grief instead of lessening it.
He spoke nothing, either good or bad, and did not even defend himself — the Chaldee having 'I ceased from the words of the law'.
He forbore to speak what he justly might, lest he break out into indecent expressions; and the silence increased the grief rather than assuaging it.

debates.question: What is the psalmist asking for in verse 4?

positions.summary: Death itself, asked in a sinful and passionate way by a man impatient of his exercises.

That God set the transitoriness of earthly life clearly before his eyes, so that he may become fully conscious of his own frailty — and so that the suffering and the prosperity of the ungodly may both be seen as short.
The words at which the dammed-up feeling finally breaks out; the reading 'how frail I am' is to be preferred, the root meaning to leave off and here implying ceasing to live.

outliers.summary: Draws a pastoral rule from the failure of the silence: mourner, tell your sorrow — first and most fully to God, but even pouring it out before a wise and godly friend is far from being wasted breath.

Collects the classical and English commonplaces of man as a shadow — Pindar, Sophocles, Horace, Burke — and sets Shakespeare beside both halves of the verse: a breath thou art, and life's but a walking shadow, a poor player.

themes: I was dumb with silence, I held my peace, even from good; and my sorrow was stirred.
My heart was hot within me, while I was musing the fire burned: then spake I with my tongue,
Lord, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am.
Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth; and mine age is as nothing before thee: verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity. Selah.
Surely every man walketh in a vain shew: surely they are disquieted in vain: he heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them.

7.pericope_label: And now, Lord, what wait I for? my hope is in thee... O spare me, that I may recover strength, before I go hence, and be no more

schools.summary: Ellicott insists on what the psalm does not have: no hope of immortality, since that had not yet dawned, so that what lifts the poet above the oppressive sense of frailty is God's mercy and the hope of his own moral deliverance. He finds the fear of the wicked's reproach grounded in the poet's own consciousness of transgression, quotes Kimchi on the double impossibility of complaint, and makes the moth image exact. Delitzsch notes only that the prayer is renewed at the end and rests on the shortness of the pilgrimage.

Gill distinguishes the silence of verse 9 from the silence of verse 2 — the first was impatience held in, this is a man who has seen the vanity of things and put his hope in God — is careful that asking for the stroke's removal does not contradict that silence, and reads the closing cry as asking God to turn away his fierce countenance.

Clarke supplies two figures: the wounded fighter of single combat who gives in and cries what our ancestors called craven, and the courtroom where God maintains the authority of his law until the culprit's guilt is proved and he faints. He wants the deliverance to serve as evidence to the godless, and answers the last plea for the psalmist, who never made this earth his home. Wesley reads the petition as asking that the judgment be lifted before he is lost, and takes the moth for God's judgments secretly consuming a people.

Henry marks the order of the petitions — pardon before relief — and the condition on which relief may be asked in faith: when our sins are pardoned and the affliction has done its work. On the submission he supplies the reason the psalm supplies: of every event we may say this is the finger of God, whoever were the instruments. Spurgeon reads the turn at verse 7 as disgust rather than despair, the psalmist cutting the cords that bound him to earth.

debates.question: What kind of turn is verse 7?

positions.summary: A disclaiming of all expectation from the world, followed by a taking hold of God: when creature-confidences fail it is our comfort that we have a God to go to.
Disgust rather than despair — the psalmist has thought on the world and all in it, is relieved that such things are passing, and cuts the cords binding him to earth.
An elevation reached without any hope of immortality, which had not yet dawned; the ground is God's mercy and the hope of moral deliverance.

debates.question: Why is the psalmist silent in verse 9 after speaking in verse 3?

positions.summary: Because this silence is different in kind: the first was impatience held in, this is a man who has seen the vanity of things and put his hope in God.
Because thou didst it — of every event we may say this is the finger of God, whoever were the instruments, and a good man has then nothing to object.
Because complaint was doubly impossible: not of man, for it was God's doing; not of God, for he was conscious of his own sin.

outliers.summary: Hears in 'remove thy stroke away from me' a figure from single combat: the fighter wounded past continuing gives in and prays his adversary to spare him, crying what our ancestors termed craven — the word spoken by the loser in the trial by battle.

themes: And now, Lord, what wait I for? my hope is in thee.
Deliver me from all my transgressions: make me not the reproach of the foolish.
I was dumb, I opened not my mouth; because thou didst it.
Remove thy stroke away from me: I am consumed by the blow of thine hand.
When thou with rebukes dost correct man for iniquity, thou makest his beauty to consume away like a moth: surely every man is vanity. Selah.
Hear my prayer, O Lord, and give ear unto my cry; hold not thy peace at my tears: for I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were.
O spare me, that I may recover strength, before I go hence, and be no more.
